title: Tattoos: Not Just For Dirtbags Anymore
summary: The hosts trace the history of tattooing from the Iceman's markings and ancient Egyptian and Nubian tattoos through Polynesian origins, sailors, Greek and Roman criminal branding, slavery and Holocaust-era marking, the Victorian elite's Japanese tattoos, Samuel O'Reilly's tattoo machine, the mid-century Golden Age, the 1960s bans, gang and counterculture tattooing, and modern trends. They then explain how tattooing works, prison tattoo methods, the tattoo process from stenciling to shading and aftercare, pain, costs, sterilization and blood-borne disease safety, MRI and tattoo risks, vegan ink concerns, henna dangers, state regulation, tattoo removal by laser and older methods, and tattoo statistics. The episode ends with listener mail about a father's leg amputation in the 1980s.

segments.title: Opening banter and website plug
segments.summary: The hosts welcome listeners, mention the Facebook, Twitter, YouTube and website, and promote a gallery of bad tattoos.

segments.title: Ancient and early tattoos
segments.summary: The Iceman's tattoos, the Egyptian god Bes on Nubian mummies, and early abstract patterns are discussed as the earliest tattoo evidence.

segments.title: Tattoos as punishment and branding
segments.summary: Greeks and Romans tattooed criminals and slaves, and tattoos were used to mark runaway slaves and later Jews and gay people in the Holocaust, with pink triangles.

segments.title: Polynesian origins and sailors
segments.summary: The word tattoo comes from a Polynesian word, introduced to the West by Joseph Banks on Captain Cook's voyage. Sailors were the first Westerners to adopt tattoos, linking them to the marginalized.

segments.title: Circus performers and tattoos as fringe identity
segments.summary: Prince Constantine, a fully tattooed circus sideshow performer, earned large sums with P. T. Barnum's circus. Tattoos stayed linked to fringe groups and were tied to outlaw images.

segments.title: Victorian elite and Japanese tattoo masters
segments.summary: After Japan reopened in 1853, Western elites, sometimes royalty, traveled to Japan to get elaborate tattoos from master artists.

segments.title: Tattoo machine and American tattoo shops
segments.summary: Early hand tattooing was slow and costly. Samuel O'Reilly's machine, based on Edison's etching pen, democratized tattoos. Martin Hildebrandt opened the first US professional shop in New York in 1846.

segments.title: Golden Age, military tattoos and 1930s oddities
segments.summary: Tattoos were linked to patriotism between the wars and WWII. People, including children, got Social Security numbers tattooed, and in the mid-1950s blood type tattoos were suggested.

segments.title: 1960s bans and counterculture tattooing
segments.summary: Hepatitis outbreaks led to tattoo parlor bans in New York City from 1961 and Massachusetts until 2000. Tattooing moved underground and was adopted by biker and Chicano gangs, and by counterculture groups in the 1970s.

segments.title: Modern tattoo trends
segments.summary: Tattoos have become mainstream since the 1980s and 1990s. Trends include UV ink and 3D nipple tattoos after breast reconstruction.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break before the hosts turn to how tattoos work.

segments.title: How tattooing works and prison tattoos
segments.summary: Ink is delivered through a needle into the dermis, which is stable, so the tattoo lasts and fades over time. Tattoo machines run from about 50 to 3000 punctures per minute. Prison tattoos are made with improvised tools like a toothbrush and staple, a modified tape player motor, and ink from boot polish or melted styrofoam.

segments.title: The tattoo process, stencils, and pain
segments.summary: Tattoo artists stencil designs on the skin because skin stretches. Work proceeds with black work outlines, then shading, then color, often in multiple sessions. Pain varies by location; bony and fleshy areas hurt more.

segments.title: Tattoo aftercare
segments.summary: Aftercare includes removing the bandage after an hour or two, gentle washing, patting dry, avoiding submersion and sun, and advice on ointment that varies between shops.

segments.title: Tattoo cost and choosing an artist
segments.summary: Tattoo prices vary widely; a 2000 survey found small tattoos averaged about forty-five dollars. Skilled artists charge more, often by the hour for large pieces. The hosts advise careful research.

segments.title: Sterilization and blood-borne disease safety
segments.summary: Tattoo parlors use single-use sterile supplies and autoclaves at high heat and pressure to sterilize reusable equipment. Indicator strips show sterility. Hepatitis risk exists; the CDC reports no HIV cases from tattoos. Skin infection is also a risk.

segments.title: MRI, vegan ink, and henna
segments.summary: Metallic pigments can burn during an MRI, and cosmetic tattoos can complicate scans. Some inks contain bone char or shellac, and some vegan issues arise. Natural henna is safe, while black henna with PPD can cause scarring.

segments.title: Tattoo regulation, blood donation, and licensing
segments.summary: The American Red Cross does not accept blood from people with tattoos in the past year unless the parlor is state regulated. Most states regulate tattoo parlors and require licensing based on a health exam, not artistic testing. Minors generally cannot be tattooed without consent.

segments.title: Tattoo statistics and extreme body modification
segments.summary: Roughly 14 percent of Americans have a tattoo, rising to about 36 percent of those aged 18 to 25. About 17 percent of tattooed people have some regret. Extreme cases include Lucky Diamond Rich and Stalking Cat.

segments.title: Tattoo removal
segments.summary: Older removal methods included dermabrasion, cryosurgery, and surgical excision. Laser removal breaks up pigment, which the immune system clears. Green is hardest to remove; blue and black are easiest. Hosts describe their own partial laser removal.

segments.title: Listener mail: father's amputation
segments.summary: Listener Amber describes her diabetic father's lower-leg amputation in Columbus, Ohio in the 1980s, performed under a spinal block with headphones playing so he could not hear the saw. He survived surgery but died that November.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite listeners to share experiences via Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
